newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's 1997 budget approved by parliament.
newsitem.headline: Italy's 1997 budget approved by parliament.

text.p: The Italian parliament on Sunday approved the centre-left government's 1997 austerity budget, drawn up in a last gasp effort to prepare for the launch of the single European currency.

The package, which aims to slice 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from next year's projected deficit, was passed at a rare Sunday sitting of the lower house of parliament by 316 votes to two, with two abstentions.

The centre-right Freedom Alliance, headed by media mogul Silvio Berlusconi, and the secessionist Northern League party boycotted the vote to protest against the bill in a final act of defiance against the contested package.

Opposition parties pinned some 10,000 amendments to the budget during its three-month battle through Italy's two houses of parliament, and the government only managed to clear it past the Senate last week thanks to a battery of confidence motions.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi breathed a sigh of relief on Sunday when the draft law finally made it to the statute book.
"We have shown where we are going and that the coalition is compact," he told state television.

Prodi, who took office in May after a general election, has said the budget will guarantee debt-laden Italy a place among the founder countries of European economic and monetary union (EMU) and has promised to resign if Italy misses the first boat.

However economists are already warning that an expected overshoot in state spending this year means that the 1997 budget will not be enough to win Italy an EMU berth from the start in 1999, adding that further action will be needed early next year if important financial goals are to be met.

The budget is designed to reduce the closely watched ratio between Italy's state deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) to 3.1 percent next year, a breath away from the three percent target established by the Maastricht Treaty for EMU aspirants.

But the International Monetary Fund predicted last week that this ratio would only fall to 3.75 percent next year from 7.1 percent in 1996, implying that some 14 trillion lire would have to be found if Italy was to meet the EMU target.
Prodi said on Friday that a decision about a mini-budget will be made in February or March, adding that any eventual initiatives would avoid tax increases.

Opposition parties have vociferously attacked the 1997 budget for leaving welfare spending unscathed and putting much of the emphasis on revenue raising plans, including an unpopular "Euro-tax" levy and a new type of regional tax for companies.
"I do not understand how anyone can be satisfied by the approval of this bill," Roberto Calderoli, secretary of the Northern League party, told reporters on Sunday.
"The people who voted in this law will be held responsible for the distruction of the productive classes," he added.
